stops.name: Los Toldos, la casa prestada en la pampa
stops.campa: On the flat pampa where the Coliqueo tolderías once stood, in a house lent to the family because the father's blood is not theirs to give, María Eva is born, the fifth and last child of Juana Ibarguren and the estanciero Juan Duarte, who keeps his lawful wife and daughters in Chivilcoy. She is entered in the registry as a hija natural, a bastard, a word that will follow her like a shadow across the plain. The wind comes off a thousand kilometres of grass. The child of no name will one day carry the name of a nation on her back.
stops.quote: Siendo una chiquilla, siempre deseaba declamar. Era como si quisiese decir siempre algo a los demás, algo grande.
stops.quote_source: Eva Perón, La razón de mi vida (1951)

stops.name: Los Toldos, la muñeca caída del camello
stops.campa: For the Day of the Kings the child asks for a doll as tall as herself. On Epiphany morning the doll arrives, but a leg is missing; her sister tells her that the Magi's camel stumbled in the night and the doll fell and broke on the road from the East. Eva holds the wounded thing and does not cry. The poor of the pampa learn early that even the gifts of kings come to them already broken, and that a broken thing may still be loved, and mended, and given a name.

stops.name: Chivilcoy, el velorio del padre, la puerta que se abre a medias
stops.campa: Juan Duarte's Chevrolet overturns on the Mitre avenue and he dies before dawn. Juana gathers her five children in mourning black and walks them to the wake at the son-in-law's house, into the presence of the lawful family. One of the estanciero's legitimate daughters rises to bar them; there is a hard word, a cold silence, but they are let in, and the bastards file past the coffin to kiss their father dead. The funeral that half-turns them away teaches Eva the exact shape of contempt. She will spend her life answering it.

stops.name: Junín, la calle Winter, el apellido Duarte tomado por bandera
stops.campa: Juana moves her brood to Junín, to a small house on Calle Ingeniero Winter, and there performs a quiet act of will: she sets aside the name Ibarguren and takes for all of them the father's name, Duarte. In a town where no one knows them they begin again, the daughters sewing and cooking and boarding lodgers, the boy Juancito clerking. Eva, thin and dark and stage-struck, recites poems at school and mimes the voices of the radio. In the pictures at the Crystal Palace cinema she sees another Argentina, luminous, and swears to reach it.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, la llegada, quince años y una valija
stops.campa: At fifteen, with a cardboard suitcase, Eva steps down into the immensity of Buenos Aires: the port city of a million lights, the theatres and the radio towers, the capital that had never once looked back at Junín. She lodges with family friends and begins the long siege of the stage doors. She is small, pale, unlettered, provincial, unbeautiful by the fashion of the day. She has, instead, a hunger that does not sleep, and a voice that the microphone will love before any audience does.

stops.name: Teatro Comedias, el debut, "muy correcta en sus breves intervenciones"
stops.campa: In the company of Eva Franco she debuts in La señora de los Pérez, a small part, a few lines. The next morning the newspaper Crítica prints the first words the world ever set down about her: muy correcta en sus breves intervenciones, Eva Duarte: correct in her brief interventions. It is nothing; it is everything. The bastard of Los Toldos has her name in the press of the capital. From here it is tours to Rosario, Mendoza, Córdoba; cheap pensions; the years of struggle in the trade she has chosen because it is the only door that opened.
stops.quote: Muy correcta en sus breves intervenciones, Eva Duarte.

stops.name: Rosario, la gira de la Compañía Argentina de Comedias
stops.campa: Contracted by the Compañía Argentina de Comedias, she goes on the road: Rosario, Mendoza, Córdoba, a four-month circuit of the provincial theatres. Third-class trains, boarding houses, a trunk of borrowed costumes, matinees for towns that will forget her by nightfall. She is learning the inland country by its stages, the same country whose poor will one day fill a square for her. The actress crosses Argentina in obscurity now; she will cross Europe in glory later; and dead she will cross the ocean itself. The wandering has already begun.

stops.name: Radio Belgrano, las biografías de mujeres ilustres, la voz de la nación futura
stops.campa: By 1943 the microphone has made her. On Radio Belgrano, in the prime hours of the night, she stars in a cycle of the great women of history: Isabel, Josefina, Catherine, Elizabeth of England. She lends her own thin, urgent voice to every queen and heroine of the past. Argentina falls asleep to Eva Duarte being someone magnificent. She is rehearsing, without knowing it, the only role that will matter: the woman who speaks to a whole people and makes them feel that something great is being said to them.

stops.name: San Juan, el terremoto, la tierra que se abre
stops.campa: At nightfall the earth convulses under San Juan and the city of adobe folds inward, ten thousand dead beneath the mud brick. From the ruin comes the colonel who runs the Secretariat of Labour, Juan Perón, calling the nation to give. The catastrophe of the west sets in motion the meeting of the east: the relief must be gathered, a great gala staged, the artists of Buenos Aires summoned. The pampa's fault line reaches, across a thousand kilometres, into a boxing arena by the river, and there it will join two lives.

stops.name: Luna Park, el festival, y el asiento junto al Coronel
stops.campa: The Luna Park fills for the benefit of San Juan: cinema, radio, tango, all of Buenos Aires giving. Eva Duarte finds her way to the seat beside Colonel Perón and does not leave it. Tradition says she turns to him and says: Gracias por existir. From this night, or from the dawn of the twenty-third, they do not part. The widower of forty-eight and the actress of twenty-four: he brings her a State, she will bring him a people. The relief of the earthquake becomes the founding of a myth.
stops.quote_source: Traditional; words attributed to Eva Duarte to Perón, Luna Park, 22 January 1944

stops.name: Isla Martín García, Perón preso, la carta de amor
stops.campa: The colonels who fear Perón's power over the workers force his resignation and lock him on the island of Martín García in the estuary, where the exiles of a century have been kept. He writes to Eva from the island as a broken and tired man who wants only to marry her and withdraw to some quiet place to live. The people's tribune is a prisoner in the river; the actress waits on the shore. But the descamisados of the meat-packing suburbs have already begun to stir, and the island cannot hold what is coming.
stops.quote: Cuando salga nos casaremos y nos iremos a cualquier parte a vivir tranquilos.
stops.quote_source: Juan Perón, letter to Eva Duarte from Martín García, October 1945 (paraphrased in the canon)

stops.name: Plaza de Mayo, el 17 de Octubre, los descamisados liberan a Perón
stops.campa: From before dawn the shirtless ones pour out of Avellaneda, Berisso, La Boca, Barracas; they cross the Riachuelo with trousers rolled and bare feet, tens upon tens of thousands, and they flood the Plaza de Mayo and will not go until Perón is freed. In the myth of the movement it is Evita who ran through the barrios rousing them, Evita who called the general strike, Evita who would not sleep until her man was returned. That night on the balcony Perón is given back to the people, and Peronism is born in the roar of the square. The bastard has become the mother of a multitude.
stops.quote_source: Eva Perón, of the workers of 17 October, in the movement's tradition
